newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Copper price strings being pulled by China.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Copper price strings being pulled by China.

text.p: World copper prices are being thrown all over the place by speculation as to whether China needs to buy the metal in the near term, and if so, how much.
Traders and analysts have made guesses based on Chinese production statistics and their own consumption estimates and come out with widely varying figures, but all pointing to import needs.
But lack of comment from official Chinese agencies has kept the market in the dark and left it open to speculative pressures.

Latest talk from within the China metals trade, however, suggests the country has ample copper to get it through the next few months which would remove a considerable prop from under the market, traders said.
Three months delivery London Metal Exchange copper was trading in the low $2,300s on Thursday but so far this year it has fluctuated widely, from $2,130 up to $2,440 a tonne.

The uncertainty in the copper market has tended to curb bull markets in zinc, aluminium and nickel where analysts had been expecting strong first half 1997 performances based on supply and demand outlooks..
Among soft commodities coffee took a backward step after recent strong performances but traders saw this as a necessary reaction to prevent the market becoming overheated.
Broker GNI said "Fundamentally coffee is still tight but we believe that the recent price hikes are too much for the market to abosorb, and further losses are likely."
Likewise cocoa appeared a little overbought and prices marked time. Contradictory reports from the world's number one supplier also took the steam out of the market, traders said.

Ivorian Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze said earlier this week that its total crop would be less than one million tonnes. But according to Ivorian industry sources, arrivals at export ports had already reached between 920,000 and 960,000 tonnes by March 7, with the season not yet over.

Precious metals were mostly steady except for palladium, which remained shakey on the possibility that the world's number one exporter of the metal, used in auto-catalysts, Russia would shortly be resuming sales after being absent from the market in 1997.
An analyst said "If they try to make up what they have lost in exports all at once, they will shatter the price.
